name: Sexual market value (SMV)

card.summary: A manosphere and looksmaxxing term for a person's overall desirability as a partner, roughly the community cousin of academic 'mate value' and 'sexual capital' ideas.
card.aka: SMV, sexual value, mate value, erotic capital (academic cousin)
card.note: SMV itself is a community concept with no standard measure; related academic research covers attractiveness, mate preferences and 'sexual capital'.

quick.overview:
Sexual market value (SMV) is slang for how desirable someone is as a sexual or romantic partner, treated as a score or rank in a marketplace. It originated on pick-up artist forums and spread through manosphere and incel-adjacent communities, where people compare themselves using decile scales, the PSL scale or a 'looks, money, status' framework. [1]

In looksmaxxing spaces SMV is the goal that appearance improvements are said to raise. Academic researchers do not use the term, but they study related ideas such as 'sexual capital', 'erotic capital' (Catherine Hakim), the pay premium for attractiveness and the matching hypothesis. [1][2]
quick.mechanism: SMV is described as a combination of traits such as facial attractiveness, height, body, status and money that determines who a person can attract. Community members rank themselves and others on numeric scales. Scholars describe related concepts, for example Adam Green's argument that desirability depends on the particular 'sexual field' and its local preferences. [1]
quick.risks: No validated instrument measures SMV, and critics of related academic theories argue that they overstate individual ownership of attractiveness and overlook culture, class and race. Community discussion also includes race-based tier lists and comparisons that scholars studying sexual racism describe as reflecting bias in dating markets. [1]

angle.text: SMV is the yardstick looksmaxxers use for what appearance work is meant to achieve: skincare, grooming, fitness, style and procedures are described as ways to raise it. The term is a community framework without a standard measure, so how much any change moves it is a matter of members' judgement.

lead: Sexual market value, usually abbreviated SMV, is a term used in manosphere, pick-up artist and looksmaxxing communities for a person's overall desirability as a sexual or romantic partner. It treats dating as a market in which each person has a comparable standing that influences the partners and attention they can attract [1][12]. In looksmaxxing it is the goal that appearance improvements are said to raise: skincare, fitness, grooming, style and surgery are all discussed as ways of 'SMV maxxing' [3].

The term is not an established concept in academic psychology. Its closest scholarly relatives are 'sexual capital' and 'erotic capital', terms sociologists and economists use for the social power a person gains from attractiveness [1][2], and the 'mate value' and matching research of social psychology [7][14]. Wikipedia reports that SMV began on pick-up artist forums and spread through incel communities to the wider manosphere [1].

Within the communities, people rank themselves and others on a 1 to 10 decile scale or the 1 to 8 PSL scale, and some use a 'looks, money, status' framework [1]. Researchers who study related ideas report that attractiveness is linked with advantages in earnings and social perception, that desirability depends on social context, and that theories of sexual capital are contested [1][2][14].

paras: In community usage, a person's SMV is a rank or score summarizing how attractive they would be to potential partners. Raters commonly use a 1 to 10 decile scale or the 1 to 8 PSL scale, and some use a 'looks, money, status' (LMS) framework that combines three metrics into one rating. Men rated near the top are called 'Chads' and those in the lower half 'sub-5' or 'incel' [1].

Posts on looksmax.org use SMV for individuals and for groups: threads rank celebrities against each other, ask what the highest SMV man on earth looks like, and debate whether the brain distorts a person's view of their own SMV [4][6][16]. Related slang such as mogging, PSL and blackpill sits around the same market framing [1][12].

Wikipedia's article on sexual capital places the origin of 'SMV' on pick-up artist forums, from which it spread to the incelosphere and wider manosphere [1]. Wikipedia's article on the manosphere traces its roots to men's-rights and pick-up-artist forums of the late 1990s and early 2000s, names Neil Strauss's The Game (2005) and Rollo Tomassi's The Rational Male (2013) as keystone works, and says the word 'manosphere' first appeared in 2009 [11].

On the Red Pill subreddit, started by Robert Fisher in 2012, the sidebar framed dating as a 'sexual marketplace' using terms like SMV; Reddit quarantined the community in September 2018 [12]. Ideas such as female hypergamy, the 'alpha fux, beta bux' model and a three-tier hierarchy of desirable, average and unattractive men became common vocabulary [11][12].

The 'black pill' emerged on incel forums as a more fatalistic variant of the red pill. Wikipedia describes it as applying the market view to looks, holding that society favours physically attractive men and that unattractive men cannot easily escape the hierarchy [12]. Looksmaxxing communities, by contrast, are organised around the idea that appearance can be changed, so SMV is discussed as something to raise rather than a fixed rank [3].

Some members push back on the framing. Threads question whether every woman has an 'unlimited' SMV and whether the brain 'lies' about one's own standing [6][9]. A woman posting on T Nation wrote that, as the pick-up artists call it, her 'sexual market value' rises when her mind is on display socially [15].

The British sociologist Catherine Hakim used 'erotic capital' from the early 2000s, presenting it as a fourth personal asset beside economic, cultural and social capital. Her 2010 article in the European Sociological Review and her 2011 book Erotic Capital argued that it is increasingly valuable in affluent societies, that it allows mobility regardless of class origin, and that women generally hold more of it than men [2]. She lists six elements: beauty, sexual attractiveness, social attractiveness, vivaciousness, social presentation (style and grooming) and sexuality [2]. The grooming and presentation elements overlap with what looksmaxxers work on.

Adam Isaiah Green's 'sexual fields' approach (2008) builds on Pierre Bourdieu and treats sexual capital as arising from attributes that draw erotic responses, with value depending on the particular field and no single dominant form; his 2014 book Sexual Fields introduced 'capital portfolios' in which sexual capital combines with economic, cultural and social capital [1]. Robert T. Michael (2004) extended Gary Becker-style human-capital thinking to sexual capital [1].

Critics say Hakim's theory, though presented as universal, mainly concerns women, ignores variation by culture and class, and treats attractiveness as more changeable than it is; Green (2013) argues it is not a portable personal possession but tied to a field, and Bay-Cheng (2015) discusses how motivations are judged in neoliberal societies [1][2].

Roy Baumeister and Kathleen Vohs proposed 'sexual economics' in a November 2004 paper in Personality and Social Psychology Review, treating heterosexual interaction as a marketplace in which women hold sex as a resource that men seek and exchange for commitment, attention or money. Critics call the theory biologically deterministic, say it relies on self-report data subject to social-desirability bias, and argue that it projects recent Western norms onto other societies and overlooks matrilineal societies [13].

No studies found. No clinical or experimental study has measured SMV as defined in community usage, and there is no validated SMV instrument. Related research on attractiveness, mate preferences and sexual capital consists of economic, sociological and social-psychological studies, described in the sections above and below [1][7][14].

Hamermesh and Biddle (1993, 1998) found that attractiveness correlates with higher income after controlling for other factors, a study of lawyers examined looks and earnings, and Hamermesh later reviewed the benefits of looks in his book Beauty Pays, attributing part of the gap to discrimination [1]. A 2002 study by Hamermesh, Meng and Zhang examined whether dress and grooming pay off [1]. Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness reports the halo effect described by Dion, Berscheid and Walster (1972), in which attractive people are credited with traits such as intelligence and honesty, and a study linking NFL quarterbacks' facial symmetry with salary [14].

The matching hypothesis, first proposed by Elaine Walster (Hatfield) and colleagues in 1966, holds that people tend to form committed relationships with partners of similar social desirability, especially physical attractiveness. Reported support comes from studies of couples; critics suggest matching may reflect fear of rejection rather than a preference for similarity. Murstein (1972) dropped self-ratings because people may rate themselves unrealistically [7].

Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness reports an OkCupid analysis of about 200,000 users (2010) in which female desirability to men peaked at 21 and male desirability to women peaked in the late 20s, and speed-dating work in which women most often chose men considerably taller than themselves [14]. It also cites work reporting that attractiveness and intelligence correlate positively [14].

Scholars summarized on Wikipedia report that in the United States white men are described as holding the most sexual capital, that Asian American men's socioeconomic success does not improve their dating prospects (Kao and colleagues, 2018), that Black men face 'sexual racism' (Smith and colleagues, 2018), and that on a gay dating app white, taller and more muscular men received more attention (Riggs, 2017; Callander and colleagues, 2016) [1]. Facial symmetry is described as nearly universally attractive, while ideals for height and weight vary by culture [1]. Green (2008) reported that low sexual capital can impair condom negotiation and produce negative emotions [1].

SMV functions as the framing for much looksmaxxing: users describe interventions as 'SMV maxxing' and debate which traits matter most [3]. Threads include celebrity 'SMV battles', a thread asking about 'the highest SMV man on the planet', race-based tier lists, and discussions of why some groups are overrepresented among self-described incels [4][5][8][10][16]. Some members use the term ironically or push back on it [6][9].

Scholars of sexual capital describe racial and gender hierarchies in dating markets as products of social context rather than fixed worth [1]. Wikipedia describes the black pill as relying on pseudoscientific claims, and researchers of the manosphere such as Debbie Ging and Lisa Sugiura offer their own critiques [11][12].

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forum members use SMV as the central measure of success, ranking people by it and arguing about what raises it [4][16].

claims.claim: Looks are the dominant component of a man's SMV.
claims.believers: Posters treat facial attractiveness as the main driver and rank celebrities and strangers by it in 'SMV battle' threads [4].
claims.experts: Research finds attractiveness associated with income and social-perception advantages, and sexual capital scholars say desirability also depends on economic, cultural and social capital and on the social field [1][14].

claims.claim: Facial and body features can be changed to raise SMV.
claims.believers: Members describe methods from muscle posing to cosmetic procedures as 'SMV maxxing' [3].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested interventions against an SMV measure, as no validated instrument exists. Studies of grooming and dress have examined earnings effects [1].

claims.claim: Race strongly shapes SMV, with tier lists of groups.
claims.believers: Threads rank ethnic groups by SMV and ask why some groups are overrepresented among incels [8][10].
claims.experts: Scholars report racial hierarchies in dating attention in some settings and describe them as products of social context and sexual racism rather than fixed value [1].

claims.claim: Perceptions of one's own SMV are distorted.
claims.believers: Members post that the brain 'lies' about one's SMV, and others complain that the community overestimates women's SMV [6][9].
claims.experts: In matching research, people may rate themselves and partners unrealistically; Murstein (1972) dropped self-ratings for that reason [7].

claims.claim: Women are hypergamous and choose partners by status and looks.
claims.believers: Red-pill and black-pill communities treat hypergamy and the 'alpha fux, beta bux' model as core [11][12].
claims.experts: Sexual economics proposes a related exchange model but is criticised as biologically deterministic and reliant on self-report [13]; Green argues desirability depends on capital portfolios and fields [1].

claims.claim: Women hold more sexual capital than men.
claims.believers: Market-framing communities often describe women's SMV as peaking early and men's as depending on looks, money and status [1][12].
claims.experts: Hakim argues women generally have more erotic capital, while critics say the theory burdens women and ignores cultural variation [2][1].

claims.claim: Personality and presentation can raise a person's market standing.
claims.believers: A woman posting on T Nation said her 'sexual market value' rises when her mind is on display [15].
claims.experts: Hakim's six elements include social attractiveness, vivaciousness and presentation [2].
